overview.text: The Tuskegee syphilis study was a U.S. Public Health Service project conducted with Tuskegee Institute in Macon County, Alabama, from 1932 to 1972 to observe untreated syphilis. It involved 600 Black men: 399 who already had syphilis and 201 who did not; participants were not deliberately infected for the study. Researchers did not obtain informed consent or offer treatment, even after it became available. Community members thought the project was a special government health-care program. After news reports and an advisory review, the study ended in 1972. Its legacy includes federal human-subject research protections and the Belmont Report, which outlined principles including respect for persons, beneficence, and justice.

key_facts.text: The U.S. Public Health Service conducted the study with Tuskegee Institute in Macon County, Alabama, from 1932 to 1972.
The study included 399 men who already had syphilis and 201 men who did not; participants were not deliberately infected.
Researchers did not obtain informed consent, and participants were not offered available treatment.
Community members understood the study as a special government health-care program.
The 1974 National Research Act established a national commission on human-subject protections; the Belmont Report, published in 1979, outlined three guiding ethical principles.
